semantics.note: 'Going to rise' is a firm forecast. 'Probably exponentially' is hedged, so that part can't be scored. The drafter's 'likely' modality tag understates how firm the rise part is, but the proposition text keeps both parts. No deadline was given.

contract.note: The contract scores the firm rise and treats exponential growth as hedged. Requiring evidence that cheaper LLMs drove the rise fits his 'which means' link. Quantity and scope are unspecified, so how they're read matters.

evidence.note: Epoch's independent price data shows LLM inference costs falling. This supports the antecedent, not the outcome, because it doesn't measure misinformation volume.

Studies synthetic images and video in Community Notes on X from Dec 2022 to Sep 2023. This is a narrow sample, not total misinformation, and doesn't link anything to text models. It shows a rise, then a plateau.

reviews.rationale: Costs did fall (e1). The packet has no representative long-run series of total misinformation volume, so the firm prediction of a rise is neither shown nor ruled out. The 'probably exponentially' part is hedged and not scored. With no deadline and no conclusive event, the claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his signed Substack letter.

semantics.note: The wording matches the source. The first clause is close to definitional. The second makes a broad point about LLMs lacking any grounding in truth, made while arguing about misinformation detection.

contract.note: The contract reads 'no way of reasoning about truth' as having no demonstrated ability to draw inferences. In context he means reasoning against an external reference standard of truth. A model that chains inferences from its own internal beliefs doesn't answer that point, so the reading is stretched against him. The date window was also the evaluator's choice.

evidence.note: The TruthfulQA paper (May 2022) uses sourced reference answers and finds models only partly truthful. It illustrates the first clause, which is close to definitional, but doesn't prove it.
Entailer (Oct 2022) builds reasoning chains from the model's own beliefs. That counts against the contract's stretched reading, not his point about lacking a reference standard of truth.

reviews.rationale: The first clause is close to definitional, not an empirical claim. The second is a broad claim about LLMs lacking grounding in truth. The contract can only score it by reading it as a denial that LLMs can chain inferences at all, which goes beyond what he said. Entailer reasons from internal beliefs, not an external standard, so it doesn't refute his actual point. On a fair reading the claim can't be tested.
